intro: Mozart wrote this concerto for a clarinet with extra low notes, not the standard orchestral instrument. William McColl plays a basset clarinet he built himself: listen to the distance between its low register and the singing upper line.
question: How does one melodic line become a conversation with an orchestra?

cues.title: A melody shaped for breath
cues.text: The slow movement opens with the solo clarinet’s melody rather than a long orchestral introduction. Across these phrases, listen for the relationship between the singing line and the space around it.
cues.evidence: The opening solo melody is specified in the score and Calvin Dotsey’s Houston Symphony account. The recording begins with a relatively quiet D-centred passage; individual breaths are not identified.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One phrase, different weight
cues.text: The opening section alternates solo phrases with fuller responses. Compare the melodic shape across the exchange: changing its weight need not mean changing the tune.
cues.evidence: The score’s opening alternates solo and ensemble. The rise in relative level around 0:35 is compatible with the first response; the analysis itself does not identify instruments.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep hearing the breath
cues.text: Throughout the opening section, listen for melodic clauses that reach a point of rest before continuing. The phrase can suggest singing without requiring an actual voice or words.
cues.evidence: This is a general phrasing suggestion. It does not claim an audible breath, a particular instrumental entrance or an event at 1:43.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The more mobile middle
cues.text: In the central section, more ornamental movement expands the solo line beyond the opening melody. Listen for how short runs remain connected to longer phrases.
cues.evidence: Dotsey describes a contrasting central section with ornamental figuration. The measured change around 2:28 suggests its approximate start in this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A wider clarinet range
cues.text: Mozart wrote the concerto for Anton Stadler’s extended-range clarinet. William McColl plays a basset clarinet of his own construction in this recording, rather than a surviving instrument from Stadler’s lifetime.
cues.evidence: The Houston Symphony account documents the extended-range instrument: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/ . McColl’s own construction is credited at https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart_-_Clarinet_Concerto_-_2._Adagio.ogg

cues.title: Ornament within the line
cues.text: Through the central span, attend to changes of register as part of the melodic phrase. A run can connect two longer notes rather than functioning as an independent display.
cues.evidence: This suggestion concerns the score’s more ornamental middle section. Greater measured activity around 3:40–4:10 supports the broad placement, not particular solo gestures.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening reconsidered
cues.text: The later return recovers the opening melody in a shortened form. Compare its familiar phrases with the more mobile middle section: recognition is part of the movement’s three-part design.
cues.evidence: The shortened return is described in Dotsey’s score account. A quieter span and a measured change around 4:22 suggest the return here; the melody has not been aligned note by note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A missing manuscript
cues.text: Mozart’s complete autograph of the concerto is lost. The early published version adapted low passages for ordinary clarinet. Modern basset-clarinet editions therefore reconstruct the extended line from surviving evidence rather than a complete original score.
cues.evidence: The lost autograph, publication changes and reconstruction problem are discussed by Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/

cues.title: A fuller returning phrase
cues.text: The return includes another fuller response. Compare its increased weight with the more exposed passages, while keeping the melodic outline in mind.
cues.evidence: The score includes an ensemble response in the return. Relative level rises around 5:40–6:05; this supports a passage estimate, not a precise orchestral entrance.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, not another episode
cues.text: The closing span extends the home-key region rather than introducing a new contrasting episode. Decoration continues, but the phrases increasingly serve the task of ending the movement.
cues.evidence: The score’s coda follows the shortened return. The drop around 6:10 and D-centred pitch estimates through 6:50 support this approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A university performance
cues.text: William McColl plays with the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra under Abraham Kaplan. The source identifies the performance as December 1987.
cues.evidence: The performers and date are stated in the Commons description: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart_-_Clarinet_Concerto_-_2._Adagio.ogg

cues.title: The closing cadence
cues.text: Near the end, the final D-major cadence and the remaining resonance complete the movement without a new extended solo episode.
cues.evidence: The score ends in D major. The recording remains D-centred around 7:20, then loses relative level through 7:30; the final attack is not precisely located.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The dominant leaves room for an answer
transitions.how: The clarinet’s first phrase comes to rest on A major, the dominant of D, rather than closing the whole paragraph on the tonic. The orchestra answers by taking up the opening melodic shape in D major. The bass renews the tonic foundation while the strings give the tune a fuller body; the Adagio’s triple pulse remains unchanged. Mozart turns a harmonic question into an orchestral reply without requiring a new theme or a modulating interlude.
transitions.evidence: The first answer is mapped at 34 s, also a measured boundary, with a level rise at 0:35. The form relation connects 3.5–19 s to 36.5–52 s. The opening phrase’s dominant ending and orchestral restatement belong to the score; the A-to-D pitch estimates support the passage placement.

transitions.title: The soloist leaves the repeated paragraph
transitions.how: After the opening paragraph has closed in D major, Mozart gives the clarinet a more mobile line in the dominant region, A major. E-major harmony now pulls towards A rather than straight back to D. The orchestra recedes into accompaniment while the soloist links sustained notes with runs and wider register changes. The tempo remains Adagio: the new motion is written into the solo note values, not supplied by turning the movement into a fast section.
transitions.evidence: The middle is mapped at 148 s, matching the 2:28 analysis boundary. The report shows the preceding D-centred close and an A-major region from about 2:30. The score supplies the dominant-key middle, ornamental solo writing and unchanged tempo; reconstructed basset notes are not individually identified.

transitions.title: The suspended dominant finds D again
transitions.how: The middle section gathers on A, now heard again as the dominant of D rather than as a home key of its own. The score’s fermata leaves room for a short solo lead-in before the original melody returns. A-major and dominant-seventh tension resolves into D major; the clarinet exchanges ornamental movement for the opening’s longer notes above restrained accompaniment. The return is shortened, so familiar material resumes without reconstructing every earlier solo-and-orchestra exchange.
transitions.evidence: The return is mapped at 262 s, the report’s 4:22 boundary. The strong A-centred 4:00–4:15 passage recedes before D-centred writing after 4:25; the form relation matches the solo return at 270–288.5 s. The dominant preparation and fermata come from the score; no particular improvised lead-in is claimed for McColl.

transitions.title: The full response releases a solo afterthought
transitions.how: The fuller orchestral response gives way to the clarinet again, but this time the solo writing extends D major instead of opening another dominant-key episode. Short ornaments and cadential turns prolong the home-key paragraph above a lighter accompaniment. A-major harmony continues to act as D’s dominant, with the bass repeatedly making the destination clear. The change in orchestral weight lets the coda sound like an afterthought to the return rather than a third contrasting section.
transitions.evidence: Coda is mapped at 372 s. Relative level drops around 6:10 after the fuller 5:40–6:05 passage, while D-centred estimates continue through 6:50. The score supplies the home-key coda and renewed solo decoration; these are passage-level timings, not aligned instrumental entrances.

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
